content: 1. The preferred treatment regimen for chancroid includes one of the following options: a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g, a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg, oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg taken twice daily for 3 days, or oral erythromycin base 500 mg taken three times daily for 7 days. 2. The diagnosis of chancroid is suggested by the presence of a painful genital ulcer combined with tender, suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy. For clinical and surveillance purposes, a probable diagnosis of chancroid can be made if all the following criteria are met: The patient has one or more painful genital ulcers. The clinical presentation, appearance of the genital ulcers, and, if present, regional lymphadenopathy are typical for chancroid. There is no evidence of Treponema pallidum infection, as determined by darkfield examination of ulcer exudate or a serologic test for syphilis performed at least 7 days after the onset of ulcers. A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test or culture for herpes simplex virus (HSV) performed on the ulcer exudate is negative. 3. Patients diagnosed with chancroid should be tested for HIV infection at the time of diagnosis. If the initial test results are negative, a serologic test for syphilis and HIV infection should be repeated 3 months after the diagnosis of chancroid. 4. Patients should be re-examined 3 to 7 days after initiating therapy. If treatment is effective, ulcers typically show symptomatic improvement within 3 days and objective improvement within 7 days after therapy. If there is no clinical improvement, the clinician should consider the following possibilities: The diagnosis may be incorrect. The patient may have a co-infection with another sexually transmitted disease (STD). The patient may be infected with HIV. The prescribed treatment may not have been used as instructed. The strain of Haemophilus ducreyi causing the infection may be resistant to the prescribed antimicrobial. 5. Sexual partners of patients with chancroid should be examined and treated, regardless of whether they exhibit symptoms, if they had sexual contact with the patient during the 10 days preceding the patient’s onset of symptoms. 6. During pregnancy, ciprofloxacin may pose a low risk to the fetus, but there is potential for toxicity during breastfeeding. Alternative drugs should be used during pregnancy and lactation. 7. Individuals with HIV infection who have chancroid should be closely monitored, as they are more likely to experience treatment failure and have ulcers that heal more slowly. These patients may require repeated or longer courses of therapy, and treatment failures can occur with any regimen. 8. For urethritis and cervicitis caused by macrolide-susceptible strains, the preferred treatment regimen is either a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g or an initial oral dose of azithromycin 500 mg followed by 250 mg orally once daily for 4 days. For patients with previous treatment failures, the preferred regimen is moxifloxacin 400 mg orally once daily for 7 to 14 days. 9. For pelvic inflammatory disease, the preferred treatment regimen is moxifloxacin 400 mg orally once daily for 14 days. 10. Sexual partners of patients with nongonococcal urethritis, cervicitis, or pelvic inflammatory disease should be managed according to established guidelines for these conditions. 11. Individuals with Mycoplasma genitalium infection and HIV infection should receive the same treatment regimen as those who are HIV-negative.
